blocks.name: Peru
blocks.lede: A lost city in the cloud forest. A green valley below it. A country worth the long way there.

bodyParagraphs: Roughly a day and a half from home, then a climb that has to be paced: Lima at sea level, Cusco at eleven thousand feet, the valley gentler in between.

Rushed, Peru is a breathless dash to a postcard. Done well, it is a slow ascent: a night or two in the Sacred Valley to acclimatise before Machu Picchu, the train timed for the quiet early hour, the high city saved for when your body is ready. We plan it around the altitude, not the calendar.

blocks.pull:
The mist clears once, briefly,
and the whole of it is there.

blocks.heading: The flights we'd secure.
blocks.lede: There is no short way from India to Lima. So the cabin and the connections are where this trip is made.
points: Ex-Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru via Europe or the Middle East then across the Atlantic: typically two stops and 24 to 30 hours, in business and first throughout.
We favour one strong long-haul partner and a single, well-spaced connection over the cheapest patchwork: flat-bed sleep on the ocean leg, a lounge at the hub, baggage checked through.
Held partner fares and award space above public prices, with the Lima arrival timed so the onward flight to Cusco runs the next morning, rested rather than rushed.
The internal hop to Cusco and the Sacred Valley transfer sequenced to your landing, with private cars on both ends: the connection never yours to chase.

blocks.heading: For Indian passports.
blocks.lede: Peru is an easier route for Indian travellers than most of South America. The conditions still matter, so we confirm your exact position before anything is booked.
points: Indian nationals who hold a valid US, Canadian, UK, Schengen or Australian visa (or permanent residence in those countries) have generally been able to enter Peru without a separate Peruvian tourist visa, for short stays: the route most of our members use.
Without one of those qualifying visas, a Peruvian tourist visa is applied for in advance through the consulate, with the usual financials, itinerary and confirmed bookings.
Either way, a passport valid well beyond your stay, proof of onward travel and confirmed hotels are expected: all of which we hold on file.
These conditions change from time to time: your advisor confirms the current requirement against your passport and visas before anything is committed; we never assume approval.

blocks.lede: Tiled light in Lisbon. A wine estate above the Douro. An ocean that runs all the way to Comporta.

blocks.note: Lisbon to begin. Then the river country of the Douro, the pine-and-dune calm of Comporta, or the cliffs of the Algarve.

We'd rather give you one base done properly: a tiled palace in Lisbon, a quinta terraced over the Douro, a sand-floor house behind the Comporta dunes, and the long, late lunches the country is built around. The difference is the season and the pairing. Arrive in the shoulder months and the famous corners feel like yours.

blocks.eyebrow: The Indian Ocean · one short flight south
blocks.name: Sri Lanka, the whole of it.
blocks.lede: Tea hills in the morning, a fort by the sea by evening. A small island, and somehow several places at once.

blocks.headingHtml: The shortest flight to somewhere else entirely.
bodyParagraphs: An hour or three from home, and the island opens: Colombo, the hill country, Galle, the south coast, each barely a few hours from the last.

The temptation is to see all of it at once. We'd rather thread three or four parts that belong together: a city night, a tea-country bungalow with a fire lit at dusk, the ramparts of Galle, a quiet southern beach to end on. Most of the work is the order and the season. Get those right, and the island never feels hurried.

blocks.heading: The flights we'd secure.
blocks.lede: The closest of the islands. A short flight, where what matters is the cabin and landing into Colombo with the day still ahead.

Business class on the wide-body services where it runs, with the short-haul flat-recline cabins SriLankan operates on the longer hops: we book the seat that suits the time of day.

blocks.heading: B1/B2, for Indian passports.
blocks.lede: The longest lead time on this list, with an interview at the US consulate. We prepare you for all of it, then stay with it until the visa is in hand.
points: A B1/B2 visitor visa is required, with the online DS-160 form, a fee, and an in-person interview at a US consulate in India.
Interview wait times in India vary widely and can run to many weeks or months: we start the moment you commit, and plan dates around the slot.
The B1/B2 is typically issued with a long validity for multiple entries, so once you have it, future US trips need no new visa.

We prepare the DS-160, assemble your documents, schedule the appointment, brief you for the interview, and track it to the issued visa. If you already hold a valid US visa, we go straight to the flights.

blocks.lede: Vietnam runs a thousand miles north to south, and the temptation is to chase all of it. We'd rather you took one stretch and took it slowly: old Hanoi and the bay above it, or the centre's lantern town and beaches, with the internal hops timed so the country never feels like a race. So much of it is the season. Come in the dry months and the whole length opens up, warm and clear.

blocks.heading: e-Visa, for Indian passports.
blocks.lede: Indian passport holders travel to Vietnam on an electronic visa. It is the quiet kind of paperwork. We arrange it in advance, so it's done before you fly.
points: Vietnam issues an e-Visa to Indian nationals, applied for online ahead of travel and valid for single or multiple entry depending on your itinerary.
We prepare the application, the photograph and the passport scan, submit it well in advance, and have the approval letter in hand before departure.
Processing usually runs a few working days; we build in margin and align the dates with your confirmed flights: your advisor confirms current requirements before you travel.
We carry the printed approval to the airport with the rest of your documents, so the immigration desk on arrival is a formality, never a worry.
